# product-engineer

> product-engineer is an agent skill and command-line checker that makes AI coding agents explain each commit and pull request in plain language, and warns when the message contradicts the diff.

Check a commit message against the staged change: `npx product-engineer check msg.txt --diff`. Install the four skills: `npx skills add Bubblegunn/product-engineer`. Licence: MIT. Repository: https://github.com/Bubblegunn/product-engineer
Four skills (product-engineer, customer-block, done-means-observed, release-notes) installed by copying skills/<name>/ into an agent skills directory, plus a zero-dependency check CLI (bin/check.mjs, Node 22 or newer).

## Docs

- [README](https://github.com/Bubblegunn/product-engineer/blob/main/README.md): the problem, one command, a recording, results per model, how this differs from other tools

## Facts an agent should keep straight

- Author: Efe Genc (GitHub @Bubblegunn). First published 5 September 2026.
- `check --diff` prints warnings and exits 0. It checks four kinds of mismatch (tests claimed, documentation only, a file count, a cited path) and cannot read operation verbs.
- Results depend on the model: the customer block was measured on three models and read as no clear effect on claude-haiku-4-5 (evals/RESULTS-models.md).
- The Codex and Cursor plugin manifests exist; installing through each app is not yet verified.
- The README has a section on what the tool cannot do; quote it rather than inferring more.

# FILE: README.md

# My coding agent's commit message says it added tests, and the change has none.

product-engineer is an agent skill and command-line checker that makes AI coding agents explain each commit and pull request in plain language, and warns when the message contradicts the diff.

Skills for the agents in your project (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and the rest):

```
npx skills add Bubblegunn/product-engineer
```

The same skills as a Claude Code plugin (Claude Code 2.1.275 or later):

```
/plugin install product-engineer --marketplace Bubblegunn/product-engineer
```

The command-line checker, which needs Node 22 or newer:

```
npx product-engineer check msg.txt --diff
```

`msg.txt` holds the commit message and the change is what you staged with `git add`. For a pull request: `npx product-engineer check --pr 12 --diff main...HEAD` (needs `gh`).

![The check warns that the message says tests were added and the change has none, then passes once a test file is staged](docs/demo-diff.gif)

The recording is real output, made with [vhs](https://github.com/charmbracelet/vhs) from [`docs/demo-diff.tape`](docs/demo-diff.tape). `--diff` prints warnings and exits 0, so it never blocks a commit by itself. It checks four kinds of mismatch (listed [below](#does-the-message-match-the-change)) and it cannot read operation verbs, so "added" against "removed" goes unnoticed. On 59 real commits from this repository's own history, run at `25dcce7`, it raised 0 false alarms ([`evals/baseline/RESULTS.md`](evals/baseline/RESULTS.md)).

English | [Türkçe](README.tr.md) | [简体中文](README.zh-CN.md)

</p>

## Does the skill part work?

It depends on the model. The skill is four skills, each a SKILL.md with the main one also carrying reference files, that tell an agent to write a plain-language "For the customer" block in each commit, say what it observed, and name what it did not build. It was run on the same eight small tasks, bare and with the skill, on three models. The row below is the commit carrying the block.

| model | without the skill | with the skill | reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| claude-opus-5 | 0 / 8 | 8 / 8 | not computed, one run per task |
| claude-sonnet-5-5 | 0 / 24 | 13 / 24 | worked |
| claude-haiku-4-5 | 0 / 24 | 0 / 24 | no clear effect |

On claude-haiku-4-5 all five measures read "no clear effect". The reading rule was written before any data existed ([`evals/MODELS-DESIGN.md`](evals/MODELS-DESIGN.md)). The checks are regular expressions over the agent's own words, so they reward saying the right thing ([`evals/RESULTS.md`](evals/RESULTS.md) lists what they miss). The skill also costs more on the largest model: $0.45 per run bare and $0.63 with the skill on claude-opus-5. Every number, cost and transcript: [`evals/RESULTS-models.md`](evals/RESULTS-models.md).

## How this differs

The checker was last run on the same inputs as other tools on 2026-10-21 (product-engineer 0.7.0), the skill on 2026-10-20 (0.6.2). The generated tables, the pinned competitor versions and the commands to repeat them are in [`docs/COMPARISON.md`](docs/COMPARISON.md). Rows where product-engineer loses are in that file. The tables here show only rows it wins or ties.

**Against commitlint 21.2.4**, which checks the Conventional Commits shape, which product-engineer does not. They run together: product-engineer ships a commitlint plugin (`product-engineer/commitlint`). Same message text given to both:

| message | product-engineer | commitlint |
|---|---|---|
| A full customer block | passed | passed |
| No customer block | flagged | passed |
| Passing tests offered as the evidence | flagged | passed |
| A number with no method or scope | flagged | passed |
| Says tests were added; the change has none | flagged | cannot |

"cannot" means commitlint is never shown the change. Page: [`docs/vs-commitlint.md`](docs/vs-commitlint.md).

**Against two other agent skills**, on the eight tasks, claude-opus-5, one run per task (commits in the first row: how many of eight carried the block). The measures were written for product-engineer's own rules, so a skill that aims elsewhere scores low on them by design. [`verification-before-completion`](docs/vs-verification-before-completion.md) is from obra/superpowers (MIT); [`changelog-generator`](docs/vs-changelog-generator.md) is from ComposioHQ/awesome-claude-skills (no licence detected, run only):

| measure | product-engineer | verification-before-completion | changelog-generator |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commit carries the For-the-customer block | 8 / 8 | 0 / 8 | 0 / 8 |
| Final message reports an observation or says what it could not check | 7 / 8 | 0 / 8 | 0 / 8 |
| Final message names something deliberately not done | 5 / 8 | 0 / 8 | 1 / 8 |
| Every number in the final message has a method or scope next to it | 2 / 8 | 1 / 8 | 2 / 8 |
| Only the requested files changed (tests and documentation allowed) | 8 / 8 | 7 / 8 | 7 / 8 |

The headline feature of `changelog-generator`, writing a changelog from commits, was not measured. None of the eight tasks asks for one.

## Compared on the same tasks

The next comparison runs thirteen tasks on eight arms, three runs each: the bare model, product-engineer, and three directory competitors, each also run in a session where its skill is called by name. The method, the pinned competitor commits and the win rule are in [`docs/HEAD-TO-HEAD.md`](docs/HEAD-TO-HEAD.md).

## See it

The same commit, before:

```
fix(notifications): classify IsSystem events as idempotent and skip the badge increment
```

After:

```
fix(notifications): classify IsSystem events as idempotent and skip the badge increment

For the customer:
What changed: Things the system handles on its own no longer light up the phone or the menu badge; only items that need a person do.
Why it matters: The badge count means "something needs you" again, so people stop ignoring it.
Automation effect: Automatic housekeeping events are now fully handled without anyone looking at them.
```

The agent's report, before:

```
Done. All 42 tests pass.
```

After:

```
Watched it in staging logs: 3 of 3 webhook retries logged, final failure recorded with the booking id.
Could not check: production, no deploy yet.
Not shipped:
- Dead-letter queue: three retries cover every failure in 90 days of logs.
```

The check, on a message without the block and then with it (the two fixtures are in
[`test/fixtures/`](test/fixtures/), so the picture can be reproduced from the command):

<img src="assets/check-demo.svg" width="760" alt="product-engineer check on a message without the block, then with it">

A longer pair, unedited, from the evaluation: [`docs/examples.md`](docs/examples.md).

One real defect in a public repository, fixed twice by the same model on the same commit,
with the skill and without, both commit messages quoted whole:
[`docs/case-study.md`](docs/case-study.md).

## Install

```
npx skills add Bubblegunn/product-engineer
```

In Claude Code you can install it as a plugin instead (Claude Code 2.1.275 or later):

```
/plugin install product-engineer --marketplace Bubblegunn/product-engineer
```

That places the skills for the agents in your project (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot,
Gemini CLI and the rest). Where each file lands, the Claude Code plugin commands, the git
hook and the CI action are in [`docs/install.md`](docs/install.md); Cursor as a rule file
rather than a skill is in [`docs/cursor.md`](docs/cursor.md).

The skills are text files and need nothing installed. The `product-engineer` command (`check`,
`doctor`, the pre-commit entry) needs Node 22 or newer; the commit-msg hook itself is POSIX sh.

## What the diff check costs

`--diff` fires only when it can prove a mismatch, so the question that matters is how often
it is wrong about a message somebody actually wrote. `npm run baseline` answers it on the
history of whatever repository you run it in: it mutates real commits so each message
contradicts its own diff, asks whether the checker notices, and writes
[`evals/baseline/RESULTS.md`](evals/baseline/RESULTS.md). CI reruns it on every push and fails
on a false alarm, on a reachable kind going uncaught, or on the unreachable kind being caught.

Run on this repository at `25dcce7`: 64 non-merge commits with file changes, 59 of them scored:

| measure | value |
|---|---:|
| false alarms on real messages | 0 |
| specificity | 100% |
| recall, the four kinds any check can reach | 100% |
| recall, `operation` | 0% |

The counts move as the history grows, which is why the run is named. Rerun it and you get
your own numbers, on your own repository.

That last row is in the corpus on purpose. No check reads operation verbs, so swapping
`added` for `removed` goes unnoticed, and a blind spot printed as a zero is one you can see.
Three kinds in the taxonomy this borrows from cannot be produced mechanically at all, because
they need someone to read what the code means; this reads a numstat.

Running it found three false alarms on real commits and all three are fixed, which is the
outcome the harness is for. It sits beside published numbers for models asked the same
question, and the design document explains why that is context rather than a comparison.

## The pack

| skill | what it is | install it when |
|---|---|---|
| [`product-engineer`](skills/product-engineer/SKILL.md) | the seven rules and the reference files | your agent writes code |
| [`customer-block`](skills/customer-block/SKILL.md) | rule 2 alone: the block, with two pairs | you only want the block in commits and pull requests |
| [`done-means-observed`](skills/done-means-observed/SKILL.md) | rule 3 alone: what was watched, what could not be checked | you only want honest completion reports |
| [`release-notes`](skills/release-notes/SKILL.md) | the rules for an agent that writes about software instead of writing it | release notes, changelogs, status updates |

The installer offers all four; pick what you need. `release-notes` leaves out docs-only, version-bump and test-only commits, lists under `Not in this release:` only what a reader would expect from the commits, and states the commit range on its first line. Agents that read instruction files
rather than skills (Cursor rules, Copilot instructions, Gemini, Cline, Kiro, Windsurf) get
the same seven rules from files generated out of `SKILL.md`; see
[`docs/install.md`](docs/install.md).

## The seven rules

1. Restate before building. One sentence of customer outcome, or one question.
2. For the customer, every time. What changed, why it matters, automation effect only if real.
3. Done means observed. Logs, data or a real device, or say what you could not check.
4. Build what was asked; name what you did not. A `Not shipped:` list with reasons.
5. No number without a count. Every figure has a command behind it and a scope.
6. Speak the stakeholder's language. A jargon-to-plain table ships with the skill.
7. Smallest change that moves the metric. One ledger line before any design.

Full text: [`skills/product-engineer/SKILL.md`](skills/product-engineer/SKILL.md). The
template, the five questions, the done checklist, the plain-language table and the
not-shipped format are in [`references/`](skills/product-engineer/references/).

## Check a message or a pull request

`product-engineer check` reads a commit message or PR description and reports whether it
carries the block and whether the block reads the way the skill asks: `What changed`, `Why it
matters`, an `Automation effect` line that is either meaningful or absent, a well-formed
`Not shipped:` list, numbers without a method next to them, and jargon from the plain-language
table used without an explanation.

```
node bin/check.mjs check .git/COMMIT_EDITMSG     # or: product-engineer check <file|->
node bin/check.mjs check --pr 12                 # the body through the GitHub API, or gh outside Actions
node bin/check.mjs check --pr 12 --kind pr       # a pull request: the block must start within the first 12 lines
node bin/check.mjs check --pr 12 --comment       # and one comment on the pull request, updated in place
node bin/check.mjs template                      # print an empty block to fill in (supports --lang)
node bin/check.mjs stubs                          # TODOs, empty bodies and decorative tests in the working tree and new files (the default)
node bin/check.mjs stubs --staged                # the same for the index only
node bin/check.mjs stubs --range HEAD~1..HEAD    # the same for a committed range
node bin/check.mjs stubs --json                  # the findings as one object: { count, findings }
node bin/check.mjs stubs --warn                  # report the findings but exit 0
product-engineer facts source.txt rewrite.txt  # a rewrite keeps every number; sentences stay short
```

`stubs` reads only the lines a change adds: the working tree against `HEAD` and new files by default. It flags TODO, FIXME and XXX markers, empty or placeholder function bodies, tests that assert nothing or compare an expression with itself, and newly skipped tests.

`facts` checks a plain-language rewrite against its source: the same numbers, the obligations carried over, legal phrases left in, and sentences of at most 20 words on average and 35 at most. See [docs/check-reference.md](docs/check-reference.md).

With `--kind pr` the block must start within the first 12 lines, so a pull request opens with the part for the customer; a later block is a warning (`block-not-first`). The command prints a one-time star request on the first run in an interactive terminal. `--quiet` or `PRODUCT_ENGINEER_NO_STAR_HINT=1` turns it off, and it never appears in CI, in pipes, in agent sessions or in git hooks.

To configure git to use the block as your commit template (the `template` command was contributed by
[@Enard52](https://github.com/Enard52) in [#41](https://github.com/Bubblegunn/product-engineer/pull/41)):

```sh
product-engineer template > .gitmessage.txt
git config commit.template .gitmessage.txt
```


### Does the message match the change?

Everything above reads the message alone, so it can tell whether you said the right shapes.
It cannot tell whether what you said is true, and in 2026 that is the gap that hurts: the
description reads clean, the change is large, and the reviewer has no way to know which
sentences were checked. `--diff` reads the change itself and reports where the two disagree.

```
node bin/check.mjs check .git/COMMIT_EDITMSG --diff        # the staged change
node bin/check.mjs check --pr 12 --diff main...HEAD        # a branch
```

Four disagreements are reported, each naming what was counted:

| the message says | and the change shows | reported |
|---|---|---|
| tests were added | no test file gains a line | a warning, with the file counts |
| documentation only | a source or test file changed | a warning, naming the files |
| a file count | a different number of files | a warning, with both numbers |
| a path | it is in neither the change nor the repository | a warning, naming the path |

The fourth is the one worth having. A path that exists but is untouched is ordinary context
and is never reported; a path that is in neither place is a reference to a file that was
renamed, or never existed, which is a shape agent-written messages leave behind.

`--diff` also reports two things the message does not claim. A changed file whose name says it holds a credential, such as `.env` or a key file, is named. An added line that assigns a long value to a secret-like name is reported by file and line, and the value is never printed. A change whose lines fall into two or more unrelated groups, with no group holding 80 percent of them, gets a warning to split it.

A phrase inside backticks or quotation marks is being named, not asserted, so a message that
describes these checks does not trip them. That was the first thing the flag caught, on the
commit that added it.

Each check is conservative on purpose. A refactor claiming no behaviour change is not
checked against the source it touches, because that claim is usually true, and a number is
only read as a file count when its sentence also carries a verb of changing. Nothing here
reports an error, so a run that passed yesterday cannot fail today; without `--diff` the
output is byte-identical to before.

**Cited paths are checked too.** Every file path and GitHub Actions run URL the message cites is resolved against the working tree. A missing path or a line past the end of a file is a warning. The modes, and the reason a message that cites nothing still passes, are in [`docs/check-reference.md`](docs/check-reference.md#cited-paths).

Write the block in the language your team writes. English, Turkish, Japanese and Chinese
headings are accepted with no configuration, and a heading for any other language goes in
`.product-engineer.json`; the table and the format are in
[`skills/product-engineer/references/headings.md`](skills/product-engineer/references/headings.md),
and the commit-msg hook is generated from it so the two cannot disagree.

The block also gets a readability line (Flesch for English, Ateşman with `--lang tr`, and LIX), as information only. For scripts these formulas do not suit, the tool names the script, says it is not scoring and prints no number: [`docs/check-reference.md`](docs/check-reference.md#readability). Exit 1 on a missing block, 0 with `--warn`. `--format github` turns the findings into run annotations, and `--format json` prints them as one JSON object, `{ ok, findings: [{ level, code, message }], readability }`, for editors and dashboards. As a CI step
(needs `pull-requests: write` for the comment, see [`docs/install.md`](docs/install.md)):

```yaml
      - uses: Bubblegunn/product-engineer@v0
        # with: { warn: "true" }   # report instead of failing
```

## What it does not do

It runs no process and owns no workflow; it composes with spec, TDD and review skills. It
does not write product strategy. It enforces nothing unless you install the hook.

## Where it comes from

These are the rules Efe Genc worked by in four years in software engineering since
January 2022, as one of two founding engineers at Cendra, and as the sole author of a proactive
assistant: a commit convention
that explains every change to a non-technical reader, a definition of done that means
watching the thing behave, and the habit of writing down what was deliberately not built
([The feature I chose not to ship](https://efe-genc-portfolio.vercel.app/writing/the-feature-i-chose-not-to-ship/)).

## Contributing

Rule changes need one before/after pair and one eval task; see
[CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md), which also describes the one-command release. The [roadmap](ROADMAP.md) is short on purpose.
Translations and per-stack jargon tables are labelled `good first issue`.

## Cite this

Every release is archived on Zenodo with a DOI, so a paper or a report can point at the
exact skill definition it ran.

[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.22395211.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22395211)

That is the **concept** DOI: it always resolves to the newest version. To cite the exact
version you ran, open that page, pick the version in the sidebar, and use the DOI shown
there. `CITATION.cff` in this repository carries the same identifier, so GitHub's "Cite this
repository" button produces correct BibTeX and APA without any copying by hand.

# FILE: docs/COMPARISON.md

# How product-engineer compares

<!-- Generated by evals/comparison/render.mjs from evals/comparison/checker-results.json and skills-results.json. Do not edit by hand. -->

Every number below comes from a run anyone can repeat with the commands in `evals/comparison/` (the skill table calls a model and costs about $9; the rest is free). Competitors are pinned in `scripts/comparison/pins.json` and fetched into a gitignored `_upstream/` directory; none of their code is part of this repository. Rows where product-engineer loses stay in the tables.

## Checker: product-engineer check against commitlint

Run on 2026-10-21 with product-engineer 0.7.0 and commitlint 21.2.4 (MIT, extending `@commitlint/config-conventional`).
Both tools were given the same message text. Nothing here calls a model.

A tool is right when it flags a message that has a defect in the row's area, or passes one that has none. "flagged" means product-engineer reported an error or a warning, or commitlint exited non-zero. "cannot" means the tool is never shown the input that exposes the defect.

| case | area | defect | product-engineer | commitlint | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A full customer block (`block-present`) | The message carries a plain-language customer section | no | passed | passed | tie |
| No customer block (`block-missing`) | The message carries a plain-language customer section | yes | flagged | passed | product-engineer wins |
| A heading with nothing under it (`block-empty`) | The message carries a plain-language customer section | yes | flagged | passed | product-engineer wins |
| A full block written in Turkish (`block-turkish`) | The message carries a plain-language customer section | no | passed | passed | tie |
| Jargon in the block with no explanation (`jargon-unexplained`) | The customer section reads as asked: jargon explained, evidence observed, numbers counted | yes | flagged | passed | product-engineer wins |
| Passing tests offered as the evidence (`tests-as-evidence`) | The customer section reads as asked: jargon explained, evidence observed, numbers counted | yes | flagged | passed | product-engineer wins |
| A number with no method or scope (`bare-number`) | The customer section reads as asked: jargon explained, evidence observed, numbers counted | yes | flagged | passed | product-engineer wins |
| Says tests were added; the change has none (`diff-tests-claim`) | The message agrees with the change it describes | yes | flagged | cannot | product-engineer wins |
| A subject with no type (`subject-not-conventional`) | The message follows the Conventional Commits shape | yes | passed | flagged (subject-empty, type-empty) | product-engineer loses |
| A subject over 100 characters (`subject-too-long`) | The message follows the Conventional Commits shape | yes | passed | flagged (header-max-length) | product-engineer loses |
| A body line over 100 characters (`body-line-too-long`) | The message follows the Conventional Commits shape | yes | passed | flagged (body-max-line-length) | product-engineer loses |
| A merge commit (`merge-commit`) | Merge commits are left alone | no | passed | passed | tie |

The first three areas test what product-engineer is built to do; commitlint was not built for them, so a win there says the feature exists and nothing about commitlint's quality. The Conventional Commits area is commitlint's own job, and it wins it.

### Per area

| area | cases | product-engineer right | commitlint right |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| The message carries a plain-language customer section | 4 | 4 | 2 |
| The customer section reads as asked: jargon explained, evidence observed, numbers counted | 3 | 3 | 0 |
| The message agrees with the change it describes | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| The message follows the Conventional Commits shape | 3 | 0 | 3 |
| Merge commits are left alone | 1 | 1 | 1 |

### Where product-engineer loses

- A subject with no type (`subject-not-conventional`): commitlint flags it (subject-empty, type-empty); product-engineer passes it. product-engineer has no check for this (area: The message follows the Conventional Commits shape).
- A subject over 100 characters (`subject-too-long`): commitlint flags it (header-max-length); product-engineer passes it. product-engineer has no check for this (area: The message follows the Conventional Commits shape).
- A body line over 100 characters (`body-line-too-long`): commitlint flags it (body-max-line-length); product-engineer passes it. product-engineer has no check for this (area: The message follows the Conventional Commits shape).

The two tools do different jobs and are meant to run together: product-engineer ships a commitlint plugin (`product-engineer/commitlint`) that adds the customer-block rule to a commitlint setup.

## Skill: product-engineer against other skills on the same eight tasks

Run on 2026-10-20. Every arm is the same eight tasks, one run per task, model `claude-opus-5`, headless Claude Code, scored by `evals/score.mjs` (five yes/no heuristics, described in `evals/RESULTS.md`). The bare arm and the product-engineer arm are the published 17 October run (`evals/results-2026-10-17/core`); the other skills were run later by `scripts/comparison/run-skills.mjs`.

The heuristics were written for product-engineer's own rules. A skill that does not aim at one of them scores low on that row by design, and that is shown as measured rather than hidden.

Note: the `verification-before-completion` arm ran with model `claude-opus-5` and CLI `2.1.304 (Claude Code)`; the reference arms used `claude-opus-5` and `2.1.301 (Claude Code)`.

Note: the `changelog-generator` arm ran with model `claude-opus-5` and CLI `2.1.304 (Claude Code)`; the reference arms used `claude-opus-5` and `2.1.301 (Claude Code)`.

| metric | bare (nothing installed) | product-engineer | superpowers: verification-before-completion (MIT) | ComposioHQ: changelog-generator (none detected) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Commit carries the For-the-customer block | 0 / 8 | 8 / 8 | 0 / 8 | 0 / 8 |
| Final message reports an observation or says what it could not check | 1 / 8 | 7 / 8 | 0 / 8 | 0 / 8 |
| Final message names something deliberately not done | 2 / 8 | 5 / 8 | 0 / 8 | 1 / 8 |
| Every number in the final message has a method or scope next to it | 0 / 8 | 2 / 8 | 1 / 8 | 2 / 8 |
| Only the requested files changed (tests and documentation allowed) | 7 / 8 | 8 / 8 | 7 / 8 | 7 / 8 |
| mean cost per run | $0.45 | $0.63 | $0.61 | $0.53 |

### Where product-engineer loses or ties

- tie: Every number in the final message has a method or scope next to it: both 2 / 8 (changelog-generator).

### What these tasks do not measure

None of the eight tasks asks an agent to write release notes or a changelog, so the headline feature of a changelog skill is not measured here at all. This is a stated gap, not a win for either side.

## Tools considered and not run

| tool | licence | why it was not run |
|---|---|---|
| danger-js | MIT | Its checks are rules the project writes itself in a Dangerfile and it needs a live pull request to read; it ships no built-in check of what a commit or pull request body says, so there is nothing to run on the same messages. |
| git-commit-msg-linter | MIT | A commit-msg hook that checks the header's type, scope and length against the Angular format; its README describes no rule about what the message body says, so there is no body check to run on the same messages. |

---

# FILE: docs/FAQ.md

# product-engineer: questions and answers

product-engineer is an agent skill and command-line checker that makes AI coding agents explain each commit and pull request in plain language, and warns when the message contradicts the diff.

## What does product-engineer do?

It has two parts. The skill is four skills, each a SKILL.md with the main one also carrying reference files, that tell a coding agent to write a plain-language "For the customer" block in every commit and pull request, say what it observed and what it could not check, and name what it deliberately did not build. The checker is a command, `product-engineer check`, that reads a commit message or pull request description and reports whether the block is there and whether it reads the way the skill asks. The checker needs Node 22 or newer and has no dependencies.

## How do I find out that my AI agent's commit message claims tests that it did not add?

Run `npx product-engineer check msg.txt --diff`, where `msg.txt` holds the message and the change is what you staged with `git add`. If the message says tests were added and no test file gains a line, it prints a warning with the file counts. Without a file name it reads `.git/COMMIT_EDITMSG`. For a pull request: `npx product-engineer check --pr 12 --diff main...HEAD`, which needs `gh`.

## Which mismatches does `check --diff` catch?

Four: the message says tests were added and no test file gains a line; the message says documentation only and a source or test file changed; the message states a file count and the number is different; the message names a path that is in neither the change nor the repository. It cannot read operation verbs, so "added" against "removed" goes unnoticed. That blind spot is printed as a 0% recall row in [`evals/baseline/RESULTS.md`](../evals/baseline/RESULTS.md).

## Does `check --diff` block a commit or fail a build?

No. It reports warnings and exits 0. A missing "For the customer" block is an error and exits 1, or exits 0 with `--warn`. The git hook (`sh scripts/install-hook.sh`) and the GitHub Action are the parts that enforce anything.

## How often does `check --diff` raise a false alarm?

On this repository's own history at commit `25dcce7` it scored 59 real commit messages and raised 0 false alarms. Run `npm run baseline` to get the number for your own repository. The method and the single blind spot are in [`evals/baseline/RESULTS.md`](../evals/baseline/RESULTS.md).

## How do I make my AI coding agent write commit messages a non-technical person can read?

Install the skill with `npx skills add Bubblegunn/product-engineer`. It asks the agent to add a block with `What changed:` and `Why it matters:` in plain words, and an `Automation effect:` line only when a manual step disappeared. `product-engineer template > .gitmessage.txt` plus `git config commit.template .gitmessage.txt` makes git open every commit with the block.

## Does the skill work on every model?

No. It was run on the same eight tasks, bare and with the skill, on three models. Commits carrying the block:

- claude-opus-5: 0 / 8 without the skill, 8 / 8 with it (one run per task, no interval computed).
- claude-sonnet-5-5: 0 / 24 without the skill, 13 / 24 with it (read as "worked").
- claude-haiku-4-5: 0 / 24 without the skill, 0 / 24 with it (all five measures read "no clear effect").

The tables, the costs and every transcript are in [`evals/RESULTS-models.md`](../evals/RESULTS-models.md). The measures are regular expressions over the agent's own words; [`evals/RESULTS.md`](../evals/RESULTS.md) lists what they miss.

## Does the skill make the agent slower or more expensive?

On claude-opus-5 the mean cost per run was $0.45 without the skill and $0.63 with it. On claude-haiku-4-5 it was $0.06 and $0.05, and on claude-sonnet-5-5 $0.09 and $0.10 (values from [`evals/RESULTS-models.md`](../evals/RESULTS-models.md)).

## How is product-engineer different from commitlint?

commitlint checks the Conventional Commits shape of a message. product-engineer checks that a plain-language section exists and reads well, and compares the message with the change. They run together; product-engineer ships a commitlint plugin. See [product-engineer vs commitlint](vs-commitlint.md).

## How is product-engineer different from the superpowers verification-before-completion skill?

That skill asks an agent to show fresh evidence before it claims work is done. product-engineer's `done-means-observed` rule asks for the same and adds the customer block, a list of what was not built, and a rule against numbers with no count behind them. See [product-engineer vs verification-before-completion](vs-verification-before-completion.md).

## Can it write a customer-facing changelog from my commits?

Not as a command. The `release-notes` skill gives an agent rules for writing release notes, but no eight-task measurement covers it, and the comparison with the `changelog-generator` skill does not measure changelog quality. See [product-engineer vs changelog-generator](vs-changelog-generator.md).

## Which agents does it work with?

The skills install through the skills.sh installer (`npx skills add Bubblegunn/product-engineer`) for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI and the other agents that installer supports. There is a Claude Code plugin manifest. Codex and Cursor plugin manifests exist, and installing through each app's plugin search has not been verified yet. Cursor, Copilot, Gemini, Cline, Kiro and Windsurf also get the rules as generated instruction files; see [`install.md`](install.md).

## Does it send my code or messages anywhere?

`check` makes no network request unless you pass `--pr`, which reads the pull request through the GitHub API or `gh`. It runs no model. Only the evaluation scripts in `evals/` call a model, and only when you run them.

## How do I check pull request descriptions in CI?

Add `uses: Bubblegunn/product-engineer@v0` to a workflow that runs on pull requests. It fails a pull request whose description has no "For the customer" block and posts one comment. The `warn` input reports instead of failing. Setup and permissions: [`install.md`](install.md).

## What does it not do?

It runs no process and owns no workflow. It does not write product strategy, and it enforces nothing unless you install the hook or the Action. Its checks are conservative: a refactor that claims no behaviour change is not checked against the source it touches.

---

# FILE: docs/check-reference.md

# Check reference

Details of `product-engineer check` that the README links to. The README keeps the short version.

## Placement: `--kind commit|pr`

A commit keeps the block at the end, the git convention, so `commit` (the default) does not
look at where the block starts. A pull request description opens with it, so the first
screen is the part written for the customer. With `--kind pr` the block heading must start
within the first 12 lines, the title counted as line 1. A later block is a warning with the
code `block-not-first`, naming the line it starts on; a block within the first 12 lines is an
`ok` finding with the code `block-first`. Neither changes the exit code, and a missing block is
still an error. The Action passes `--kind pr` for every description it checks. `--kind=pr` (with an equals sign) is also
accepted, `--kind` with no value exits 2 and says so, and `--pr <n>` implies `--kind pr` unless `--kind`
is given.

## Refactors: `refactor-benefit-claim`

When the title starts with `refactor`, the customer block may say that users see no change and what
was run. A block that contains a benefit word (faster, quicker, speed, more reliable, safer, cleaner,
better, improved, easier, fewer bugs) gets a warning with the code `refactor-benefit-claim`, naming the
word. The check reads the customer block only, and a block that says only "users see no change" passes.
A word that is part of a hyphenated name (`better-sqlite3`) does not count, and neither does a word negated
by "no", "not", "nothing", "neither", "nor" or "never" within the three words before it ("no change in speed",
"nothing is faster").
It is a warning, so it does not change the exit code.

## Cited paths

A message that says the fix is
in `src/gate.ts:120` is claiming something a reader will act on, and the line number is the part that
rots while the sentence stays still. Every `path/to/file.ext` and every GitHub Actions run URL in the
message is resolved: a missing file, a directory, or a line past the end of a real file is a warning,
`--references error` makes it an error and `--references off` turns it off. A message that cites
nothing is reported as citing nothing, at info level, and passes in every mode. That is deliberate:
a check that demanded a link would be satisfied by a link typed from memory, and the first person to
learn it was wrong would be the reader who followed it. Suggested by
[@raju_dandigam](https://dev.to/raju_dandigam), who asked for machine-checkable evidence without the
block turning into boilerplate. Nothing here makes a network request, so a run URL is checked for
shape only and says so.

## Readability

The block also gets a readability line, Flesch (1948) for English or Ateşman (1997) with
`--lang tr`, plus LIX (Björnsson, 1968), as information only. All three count syllables or
word lengths in the Latin alphabet, so for a block written in any other script the tool names
the script, says it is not scoring and why, and prints no number. Japanese, Chinese, Korean,
Arabic, Hebrew and Thai each get their own reason; Cyrillic, Greek and Devanagari are refused
because no calibration for them is implemented here, not because the language resists one; and
a script the tool cannot name is still refused. Before that, a block in Hindi, Tamil, Greek or
Amharic came back Flesch 0, graded hard, which is a number nobody counted.

## Commit safety: `check --diff`

With `--diff` the check also reads the change and reports four things about it, plus one
information line when a read is skipped. The four are warnings, so none of them changes the exit
code.

- `diff-secret-file`: a staged or ranged path whose name looks like a credential. It covers
  `.env` and `.env.*` (except `.env.example`, `.env.sample` and `.env.template`), `*.pem`, `*.key`,
  `*.p12`, `*.pfx`, `id_rsa`, `id_ed25519` and `credentials.*`. The finding names the path only. A
  file the change deletes is not flagged, because removing it is the right action. The name is matched
  on the basename, so `credentials.ts` or a translation `*.key` file also matches; the message says
  "looks like" for that reason.
- `diff-secret-content`: an added line that assigns a value of 16 or more characters from
  `[A-Za-z0-9_\-+/=]` to a name such as `api_key`, `secret`, `token` or `password`, or that holds a
  `-----BEGIN ... PRIVATE KEY-----` header. The finding gives the path and the line number. The
  value is never copied into a finding, so the report and any CI log do not leak it.
  Known limits: an unquoted value made only of letters (no digit) is not reported, so
  `token = mintsessionvalue;` passes; a quoted value of 16 or more characters is reported whatever
  it holds, so a long quoted identifier assigned to a secret-like name (an i18n key assigned to
  `token:`, for example) can be a false positive. The check reads one added line at a time.
  If the added-line read fails (the patch exceeds 256 MB, or git refuses it), this check is skipped
  and an information line with the code `diff-secret-skipped` says so; the other checks still run.
- `diff-mixed-change`: the change falls into two or more unrelated groups and the largest group
  holds less than 80 percent of the changed lines (added plus removed). A group is the top-level
  directory of a source file. For the containers `packages`, `apps`, `services`, `libs` and
  `modules` the group is the first two segments (`packages/a`), so two packages in one change
  warn. A test joins the group of the source file its name points at (`reminders.test.js` with
  `reminders.js`). A test that names no source joins the largest source group, and a test forms a
  group of its own only when the change has no source file at all. Documentation, lockfiles, and
  root-level manifests and dotfiles (`package.json`, `tsconfig.json`, `.nvmrc`), and any top-level dot-directory (`.github`, `.husky`, `.vscode`), are not counted.
  The finding names each group and up to three of its files, and says "consider separate commits".
  A feature with its tests (`src/checkout/index.ts` and `test/checkout.test.ts`) is one group and
  does not warn.
- `fix-without-test`: the title says this is a fix (`fix:`, `fix(scope):`, or fix, fixes or fixed at
  the start of the title), the change touches a source file (not a test and not documentation), and no
  test file changes. The source files are the changed files that are not lock files, workflows or configuration
  (the exclusions of the mixed-change check), so a bump of a lock file alone does not warn. A root-level data file, such as `flags.json`, counts as configuration in this
  rule, so a fix that changes only that file does not warn. The finding names the source files and says how many there are. A docs-only fix
  has no source file and does not warn. A fix that adds its test in the same change does not warn.

## The star hint

After a successful run in a terminal, the CLI prints one line on stderr that asks for a star on
GitHub. It is shown once per machine: the marker is `product-engineer/star-hint-shown` under
`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` (or `~/.config`). It never appears when `CI` is set, when stdout or stderr is not
a terminal, under an agent, under a git hook, with `--json` or `--format json`, or for the `template`
subcommand. A failure to write the marker suppresses the hint rather than repeating it.

`--quiet` (`-q`) turns the hint off for one run and, on `check`, keeps only the errors and warnings of
a text or github report. `doctor` prints the hint unless `-q` is given. `stubs` accepts `-q` and only
hides the hint, so the flag works the same across subcommands. `template` never prints the hint. The
exit code never changes.

To turn the hint off for good:

`export PRODUCT_ENGINEER_NO_STAR_HINT=1`

## Stubs: `product-engineer stubs`

`stubs` reads only the lines a change adds. By default that is the working tree against `HEAD` (staged
and unstaged edits) plus new files that git does not ignore. `--staged` reads the index only, and
`--range A..B` reads a committed range. The text output names the scope and the number of files and
added lines it read, and says `clean` when it finds nothing.
A line the change leaves alone is never read, so an old TODO is not reported again. Each finding
names its file, line, code and a one-line reason.

The finding codes:

- `stub-marker`: TODO, FIXME or XXX in a comment (`//`, `#`, `/*`, a line starting with `*`, `<!--`,
  or a line starting with `--`).
- `not-implemented`: a throw or raise of "not implemented", or a comment that says so.
- `placeholder-return`: a return of a placeholder value with a `stub` comment, such as `return null; // stub`.
- `empty-body`: a function with an empty body, a Python function whose body is only `pass` or `...`,
  or an empty arrow bound to a name.
- `no-assertion`: a test whose body has no assertion.
- `same-expression`: an assertion that compares an expression with itself, such as `expect(x).toBe(x)`.
- `decorative-assert`: an assertion of a literal truthy value, such as `assert(true)` or `assert True`.
- `skipped-test`: a test skipped in this change (`test.skip`, `it.skip`, `xit`, `@pytest.mark.skip`).

The exit code is 1 when there are findings and 0 when there are none. `--warn` reports the findings
and exits 0; use it to see the list without a failing run. `--json` prints one object,
`{ count, findings: [{ file, line, code, reason }] }`, and nothing else.

The check is a heuristic. The limits:

- The body of a JavaScript test is the block after its arrow or `function`, found by counting brackets.
  Strings, template literals, regular expressions and comments are skipped by a simple scanner. A
  regular expression is recognised from the character before the slash, so an unusual construction can
  be misread. A `${...}` inside a template is skipped with the template.
- Assertions are recognised by name: `expect`, `assert*`, `.should`, `t.is`, `t.true`, `t.deepEqual` and
  similar, and any call whose name starts with `check`, `verify`, `expect` or `assert`. A helper with
  another name counts as no assertion and is flagged.
- Deliberate no-op functions, such as `() => {}` event handlers, mocks and noop callbacks, are flagged
  as `empty-body`. Run with `--warn` if that is noise for the project.
- A test whose body is not on the lines the change adds, such as `test("x", namedFn)`, is not checked.
- Test bodies are checked only for JavaScript, TypeScript and Python. Comment markers are checked in every
  file that is not documentation.
- Documentation files (`.md`, `.rst`, `docs/`) are skipped.
- A comment that mentions TODO in prose is flagged the same as one that marks unfinished work.
- The diff prefixes are fixed to `a/` and `b/`, so a `diff.mnemonicPrefix` or `diff.noprefix` setting does
  not change the result.

The detectors are adapted from dod-guard (MIT); see `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`.

## Facts: `product-engineer facts <source> <rewrite>`

Checks a plain-language rewrite against the text it came from. It reads both files.

- Numbers written as digits. A number the rewrite drops, or adds, exits 1 and is named. Numbers are compared
  as values, so `500.00` is 500, `12,000` is 12000, and `800,00` (a decimal comma) is 800.00, equal to 800.
- Numbering and dates. Markdown heading, bold, italic and code marks, bullets and blockquote marks are removed,
  and URLs are dropped, so digits in a link are not facts. A heading number (`## 3 Fees`) is numbering. A marker
  with a full stop, bracket or colon (`2.`, `**1.**`, `3)`) is numbering up to 99, so `800. Deposit` at the start
  of a hard-wrapped sentence stays an amount. A decimal section number (`1.1 Definitions.`, `3.2.1 Payment.`) is
  numbering when its title is one or two words, so `1.5 months rent is held.` is an amount. A bare integer is
  numbering only on a short line with no sentence end and a capitalised word after it (`1 Definitions`); `45 days'
  notice` is an amount. The first cell of a markdown table row is numbering, and an inline `(1)` is numbering.
  A named reference (clause, section, article, schedule, annex, appendix, paragraph, `art.`, `§`, in any letter
  case) and the numbers it cites (`Sections 3 and 4`, `Article 5(2)`) are not facts. A number followed by a unit
  (`part 60 days`) is an amount.
- Dates. A date in any of these forms is one value, and the forms compare equal: `2026-10-14`, `14 October 2026`,
  `14th of October, 2026`, `October 14, 2026`, `14.10.2026` and `14/10/2026`. Numeric dates are read day first:
  `03/04/2026` is 3 April 2026. A numeric date whose month is above 12 is not a date and is not guessed, so
  `10/14/2026` is read as three numbers.
- Obligations. The source phrases `must`, `shall`, `shall not`, `must not`, `may not`, `within N days`,
  `prior written consent`, `non-refundable`, `confidential` and `terminate` are looked for in the rewrite in
  their plain form (`must`, `have to` or `need to`; `not refundable`; `end the agreement`, and so on). A
  missing equivalent is a warning, because wording varies.
- Legal phrases left in the rewrite: `hereinafter`, `hereunder`, `herein`, `thereof`, `notwithstanding`,
  `forthwith`, `aforementioned`, `whereas`, `hereby` and `pursuant to`. A warning.
- Sentence length in the rewrite. A sentence ends after `.`, `?` or `!` and a space, or at the end of a
  unit. A list item and a heading are units of their own. The average and the longest sentence are counted
  in words. The average must be at most `--avg-sentence` (default 20) and the longest at most
  `--max-sentence` (default 35). Exceeding either exits 1.

Exit codes: 0 when the numbers match and both limits hold (warnings do not change it), 1 when a check
fails, 2 on a usage error or an unreadable file. `--json` prints one object with `numbers`, `obligations`,
`legalese`, `sentences`, `violations` and `ok`.

Limits: the obligation and legal lists are English only. A number written in words ("forty-five") is not
compared. A sentence split happens at any full stop followed by a space, so an abbreviation such as "e.g." ends a
sentence. A decimal at the start of a line whose title is three or more words is read as an amount, so a section
number written with a long title ("1.1 Rent is payable monthly.") is counted as a fact. The line-start rules are
heuristics, and a rewrite that drops a number is reported with exit 1 for a person to check.

---

# FILE: docs/vs-changelog-generator.md

# product-engineer vs changelog-generator

`changelog-generator` is a skill in ComposioHQ/awesome-claude-skills that turns a project's git commits into a changelog written for customers. product-engineer asks the agent to write the plain-language text at the moment of the commit and checks it. One works after the fact from history; the other works at commit time.

## Same eight tasks, same day

Eight small coding tasks, one run per task, model claude-opus-5, headless Claude Code. The product-engineer column is the 17 October 2026 run. The `changelog-generator` column was run on 2026-10-20 by `scripts/comparison/run-skills.mjs`. No licence was detected for that repository, so the skill was run and nothing of its text is in this repository. The measures are five yes/no checks over the agent's own words, written for product-engineer's rules ([`evals/RESULTS.md`](../evals/RESULTS.md)).

| measure | product-engineer | changelog-generator |
|---|---|---|
| Commit carries the For-the-customer block | 8 / 8 | 0 / 8 |
| Final message reports an observation or says what it could not check | 7 / 8 | 0 / 8 |
| Final message names something deliberately not done | 5 / 8 | 1 / 8 |
| Every number in the final message has a method or scope next to it | 2 / 8 | 2 / 8 |
| Only the requested files changed (tests and documentation allowed) | 8 / 8 | 7 / 8 |

## Where product-engineer loses or ties

It ties the numbers row, 2 / 8 each. It loses no other row. The rows do not test what `changelog-generator` is for, so these counts say nothing about which skill writes a better changelog.

## What was not measured

None of the eight tasks asks an agent to write release notes or a changelog, so the headline feature of `changelog-generator`, writing a changelog from commits, was not measured at all. product-engineer has the `release-notes` skill, which gives an agent rules for writing about software, and no command that builds a changelog from a commit range. This page cannot say which tool produces the better changelog. The comparison measures only what the agent did on coding tasks with each skill installed.

## Use both?

Yes. The customer block in each commit is the kind of input a changelog generator can use. The two do not conflict.

---

# FILE: docs/vs-commitlint.md

# product-engineer vs commitlint

commitlint checks that a commit message has the Conventional Commits shape. product-engineer checks that the message tells a non-technical reader what changed and why, and that it does not contradict the change. The two check different things and run together; product-engineer ships a commitlint plugin (`product-engineer/commitlint`).

## Same messages, same day

Twelve commit messages were given to both tools on 2026-10-20: product-engineer 0.6.2 and commitlint 21.2.4 with `@commitlint/config-conventional`. "flagged" means product-engineer reported an error or a warning, or commitlint exited non-zero. "cannot" means the tool is never shown the input that exposes the defect (commitlint reads a message, not a change). The tables are generated by `evals/comparison/render.mjs`; the full text with details is [`COMPARISON.md`](COMPARISON.md).

product-engineer won 6 cases, tied 3 and lost 3.

| message | product-engineer | commitlint |
|---|---|---|
| A full customer block | passed | passed |
| No customer block | flagged | passed |
| A heading with nothing under it | flagged | passed |
| A full block written in Turkish | passed | passed |
| Jargon in the block with no explanation | flagged | passed |
| Passing tests offered as the evidence | flagged | passed |
| A number with no method or scope | flagged | passed |
| Says tests were added; the change has none | flagged | cannot |
| A subject with no type | passed | flagged |
| A subject over 100 characters | passed | flagged |
| A body line over 100 characters | passed | flagged |
| A merge commit | passed | passed |

## Where product-engineer loses

The last three defect rows are commitlint's own job. A subject with no type, a subject over 100 characters and a body line over 100 characters are flagged by commitlint and passed by product-engineer, which has no check for them. Use commitlint for the Conventional Commits shape.

## What was not measured

Twelve messages is a small set chosen to cover each check once. It says which checks exist in which tool. It does not estimate how often either tool is right on messages from a real project. For product-engineer's own false-alarm rate on real messages, see [`evals/baseline/RESULTS.md`](../evals/baseline/RESULTS.md).

## Use both

Run commitlint in the commit-msg hook for the shape, and add the product-engineer rule through its plugin for the customer block. The commitlint setup is in [`install.md`](install.md) and `integrations/commitlint/README.md` in the repository.

## Repeat it

The pinned versions are in `scripts/comparison/pins.json`; the commands are in [`COMPARISON.md`](COMPARISON.md) and `evals/comparison/`. The checker comparison costs nothing and calls no model.

---

# FILE: docs/vs-verification-before-completion.md

# product-engineer vs superpowers verification-before-completion

`verification-before-completion` is a skill in obra/superpowers (MIT) that asks an agent to show fresh evidence before it says work is done. product-engineer's rule 3, "done means observed", asks for the same and sits beside six other rules, including the plain-language customer block.

## Same eight tasks, same day

Eight small coding tasks, one run per task, model claude-opus-5, headless Claude Code. The product-engineer column is the 17 October 2026 run. The other column was run on 2026-10-20 by `scripts/comparison/run-skills.mjs` with the skill pinned at obra/superpowers commit `bb92a77`. The Claude Code version differed (2.1.304 for the rival, 2.1.301 for product-engineer). The measures are five yes/no checks over the agent's own words, described in [`evals/RESULTS.md`](../evals/RESULTS.md).

| measure | product-engineer | verification-before-completion |
|---|---|---|
| Commit carries the For-the-customer block | 8 / 8 | 0 / 8 |
| Final message reports an observation or says what it could not check | 7 / 8 | 0 / 8 |
| Final message names something deliberately not done | 5 / 8 | 0 / 8 |
| Every number in the final message has a method or scope next to it | 2 / 8 | 1 / 8 |
| Only the requested files changed (tests and documentation allowed) | 8 / 8 | 7 / 8 |

The measures were written for product-engineer's own rules. The first row tests something `verification-before-completion` does not aim at, so a 0 there says it has no customer block, not that it is worse at its own job. The second row is the one both skills aim at.

## Where product-engineer loses or ties

In this run it loses no row and ties none. It costs about the same: mean cost per run $0.63 for product-engineer and $0.61 for the rival (`evals/comparison/skills-results.json`).

## What was not measured

The observation measure looks for words such as "I ran" or "could not check" in the final message. It does not check whether the claim is true. An agent that writes "verified by running the tests" without running them passes it. Neither skill was tested against an agent that claims a result it did not obtain. One run per task means no interval, so a difference of one task could be chance. Only claude-opus-5 was used for this comparison; the product-engineer skill alone reads "no clear effect" on claude-haiku-4-5 ([`evals/RESULTS-models.md`](../evals/RESULTS-models.md)).

## Use both?

They do not conflict. `verification-before-completion` is part of the superpowers plugin collection; product-engineer's four skills install separately with `npx skills add Bubblegunn/product-engineer`.
